prompt: Where do the planner's files come from when the Capacitor app runs on a phone?

choices.text: From your computer's dev server, over the network
choices.why: That is live reload, which the lesson says never ships.

choices.text: From inside the app itself
choices.why: Right. Capacitor serves them from the app's own files.

choices.text: From Capacitor's servers, the first time the app opens
choices.why: Capacitor runs no servers for your app.

choices.text: From the store, on every launch
choices.why: The store delivers the app once; the files are inside it.

prompt: Match each platform to the origin Capacitor serves the app at.

pairs.left: npm run dev in a browser

prompt: The planner calls fetch("http://localhost:3000/api") inside the Capacitor app on a phone. What does it reach?

choices.text: The developer's computer, through Capacitor's bridge
choices.why: The bridge carries plugin calls, not network requests to your computer.

choices.text: Your API, because the origin is localhost too
choices.why: Sharing the name does not share the machine.

choices.text: Port 3000 of the phone itself
choices.why: Right. On the phone, localhost is the phone; an API needs its real address.

choices.text: The store's proxy
choices.why: There is no such proxy.

prompt: Why can this course run most of a plugin's behaviour in Chromium?

choices.text: Most official plugins ship a web implementation
choices.why: Right, such as Preferences writing to localStorage.

choices.text: Chromium contains the native code of Android's plugins
choices.why: It does not; Android's WebView is built on Chromium, not the other way round.

choices.text: Capacitor emulates a phone inside the browser
choices.why: Nothing is emulated; the web implementation is a third, separate one.

choices.text: Playwright installs the native plugins
choices.why: Playwright only drives the browser.

prompt: A team edited a file in Xcode, and the next build of their old Cordova app lost it. Why would the same edit survive in Capacitor?

choices.text: Capacitor backs up Xcode files before each build
choices.why: There is no backup; there is no regeneration to need one.

choices.text: Capacitor forbids editing native files
choices.why: The opposite: they are yours to edit.

choices.text: The project is generated once and is source from then on
choices.why: Right. It lives in git, and sync only refreshes the copied web files.

choices.text: Xcode keeps the old version
choices.why: Xcode is not the reason.

prompt: Why is @capacitor/cli installed with -D and @capacitor/core without it?

choices.text: The CLI is larger
choices.why: Size is not the reason.

choices.text: The app imports core; nothing in it imports the CLI
choices.why: Right. The CLI is the cap command you run on your computer.

choices.text: -D makes the CLI available inside the WebView, where the app can call it
choices.why: The opposite: -D keeps it off the phone.

choices.text: core is only needed on iOS
choices.why: Both platforms use it.

prompt: npm reports three moderate vulnerabilities after installing @capacitor/cli. What does the lesson advise?

choices.text: Run npm audit fix --force so the warnings go away
choices.why: --force may move packages across major versions and leave Capacitor's packages mismatched.

choices.text: Remove the CLI and add platforms by hand
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests that.

choices.text: Read npm audit; they are in a tool, not in what ships
choices.why: Right. A -D package runs on your computer and never reaches the phone.

choices.text: Downgrade Node to 18
choices.why: Node is not involved.

prompt: Six months after publishing, a developer changes appId from com.example.studyplanner to com.ana.planner. What happens in the stores?

choices.text: It is a different app, with no installs and no update path
choices.why: Right. The appId is the app's identity in both stores.

choices.text: The store renames the existing listing
choices.why: The listing is keyed by that identity.

choices.text: Nothing changes; the appId is only the label under the icon
choices.why: That is appName.

choices.text: Users get the new app as an update
choices.why: An update needs the same identity.

prompt: For a Vite project, webDir in capacitor.config.ts is ___.
The app opens on the phone to a white screen right after cap add. Which cause does the lesson name as the most common?

choices.text: The phone's WebView is too old to draw HTML
choices.why: Not the cause the lesson names.

choices.text: A wrong webDir
choices.why: Right. The folder it copied holds no index.html.

choices.text: A missing appName
choices.why: cap init does not run without one.

choices.text: The bridge failed to start
choices.why: A bridge failure does not blank a working page.

prompt: Which of these does Capacitor's cap add android do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: writes a native Android project
choices.why: Into android/.

choices.text: copies dist/ into it
choices.why: Into app/src/main/assets/public.

choices.text: builds an APK
choices.why: Building is Gradle's job, later.

choices.text: installs the Android SDK
choices.why: It does not; lesson 3 does.

prompt: Do android/ and ios/ go into git?

choices.text: No, they are generated and belong in .gitignore
choices.why: They are generated once and edited afterwards, which makes them source.

choices.text: Yes, they are source you will edit
choices.why: Right. Icons, permissions and native code are changed there.

choices.text: Only android/, since ios/ needs a Mac
choices.why: Both go in; needing a Mac to build does not change that.

choices.text: Only their build/ folders
choices.why: build/ is precisely what is ignored.

prompt: On the recording machine, cap doctor said Android looked fine. What did that not check?

choices.text: That the versions of the packages match
choices.why: It checked that; it prints them.

choices.text: That an Android SDK exists
choices.why: Right. It only means the project is in order.

choices.text: That android/ exists
choices.why: It does look at the project.

choices.text: That Xcode is installed
choices.why: It checked that, and reported the error.

prompt: What does the iOS project use to pull in Capacitor's native code?

choices.text: Gradle
choices.why: That is Android's build tool.

choices.text: Swift Package Manager, through Package.swift
choices.why: Right. cap add ios wrote Package.swift.

choices.text: npm, inside Xcode
choices.why: npm installs the JavaScript side.

choices.text: A copy of Capacitor placed in public/ at every sync
choices.why: public/ holds your web files.

prompt: Put the steps that take a change to the phone in order.
items: the native build in Android Studio or Xcode

prompt: After the sed, cap sync ran and the Android copy still said All courses. Why?

choices.text: dist/ had not been rebuilt
choices.why: Right. sync copied dist/, which was built before the edit.

choices.text: cap sync only updates iOS unless told otherwise
choices.why: It was given android and updated it.

choices.text: The sed failed silently
choices.why: The rebuild then showed Back to courses.

choices.text: Gradle caches web files
choices.why: Gradle never ran.

prompt: What is capacitor.config.json inside android/app/src/main/assets?

choices.text: A file you edit to configure Android
choices.why: It is rewritten on every copy.

choices.text: The Gradle build settings
choices.why: Those are the .gradle files.

choices.text: The TypeScript settings, rewritten for Java and Swift
choices.why: Right. It is capacitor.config.ts as JSON, because neither Java nor Swift reads TypeScript.

choices.text: A list of the planner's courses
choices.why: That is courses.json, in public/.

prompt: You add a new Capacitor plugin to package.json and change no web code. Which command does the lesson's reasoning point to?

choices.text: npx cap copy, since nothing in dist/ changed
choices.why: copy does not install the plugin's native side.

choices.text: npx cap sync
choices.why: Right. sync is copy plus update, and update installs the plugin's native side.

choices.text: npx cap add android again
choices.why: The project already exists, and add would refuse.

choices.text: npm run dev
choices.why: That serves the site; it touches no native project.

prompt: What does live reload on a phone need? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: phone and computer on the same network
choices.why: The phone has to reach the computer.

choices.text: the dev server listening on that network
choices.why: npm run dev -- --host.

choices.text: Android allowing plain http for that address
choices.why: cleartext: true.

choices.text: server.url set to localhost
choices.why: On the phone, localhost is the phone.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer cap run android --live-reload to editing server.url in the file?

choices.text: It reloads faster
choices.why: Speed is the same.

choices.text: It works without the dev server
choices.why: It needs the dev server like the other.

choices.text: It encrypts the connection to the dev server for you
choices.why: Nothing in it adds encryption.

choices.text: The setting lasts one run and never reaches git
choices.why: Right. A committed server.url can end up in a release.

prompt: A release build went out with server.url still set. What do users who install it get?

choices.text: The planner, since dist/ is inside the app as well
choices.why: With server.url set, the WebView opens that address instead of the bundled files.

choices.text: A WebView opening an address on the developer's network
choices.why: Right: nothing, or somebody else's computer, on their network.

choices.text: An error from the store at install time
choices.why: Installation works; the app is what breaks.

choices.text: Live reload from the developer's laptop
choices.why: Only on that laptop's network, and only while it runs.

prompt: Which file is the one decision in this lesson you cannot take back?

choices.text: The webDir
choices.why: It can change whenever the build folder does.

choices.text: The app's name under the icon
choices.why: appName can change later.

choices.text: The appId
choices.why: Right. It is the app's identity in both stores.

choices.text: Whether android/ is committed
choices.why: That can be changed with any commit.
